cards.t: What diuretics do (salt and water balance)
q: what is a diuretic
how do diuretics make you urinate more
why does water follow sodium
cards.x:
A diuretic is a drug that increases urine flow and the amount of sodium and chloride you excrete. It works by blocking the kidney from taking sodium and chloride back into the blood. The rule that explains it: wherever salt goes, water wants to follow, so salt left behind in the urine pulls water into the urine with it.

The goal is a middle zone. Too much sodium and water means volume overload, including pulmonary edema (fluid backed up in the lungs). Too little means volume depletion and, at the extreme, cardiovascular collapse. A sustained imbalance between sodium and chloride intake and loss is fatal either way, so a diuretic is meant to nudge the body back toward the middle.

cards.t: Diuretic braking (the kidney fights back)
q: what is diuretic braking
why do ACE inhibitors work well with diuretics
how does the body respond to a diuretic
cards.x:
Diuretic braking is the kidney's way of resisting a diuretic. The kidneys need their blood flow and don't like losing volume. So when a diuretic drains salt and water, they switch on compensating mechanisms to prevent volume depletion and cardiovascular collapse. These are:
- The sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system are activated.
- Blood pressure falls, so there is less pressure natriuresis (the salt loss that pressure normally drives).
- Atrial natriuretic peptide falls while antidiuretic hormone rises.
- Kidney cells grow larger (hypertrophy).

The result is that the diuretic works less well than it otherwise would. That is why angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and calcium channel blockers pair well with diuretics. They block some of those compensations, so the combination is synergistic.

cards.t: Where each diuretic class works along the nephron
q: which part of the nephron does each diuretic act on
why are loop diuretics the most potent
why are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors the weakest diuretics
cards.x:
Each diuretic class works at its own stretch of the nephron (the kidney's filtering and processing tube). The amount of sodium handled there tracks how strong the drug is:
- Proximal tubule: 60 to 70 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed here. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act here.
- Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle: about 25 percent of the sodium. Loop diuretics.
- Distal tubule: about 5 percent. Thiazide diuretics.
- Collecting duct: 2 to 3 percent. Potassium-sparing diuretics, and aldosterone antagonists act at this end too.

So loops are the most potent, then thiazides, then potassium-sparing drugs and aldosterone antagonists. The carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are the exception. They act where most of the filtrate is reabsorbed, yet they are the weakest, because everything downstream makes up for them. The percentages are for recognition; what matters is which class works where.

cards.t: How the nephron handles water (loop limbs, antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone)
q: which limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water
what controls water in the collecting duct
what is the difference between aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone in the kidney
cards.x:
Water and salt are not handled the same way all along the nephron. In the descending limb of the loop of Henle, water leaves the tube. The thick ascending limb is the opposite: it is impermeable to water, like a waterproof wall, so sodium is taken back there without water following.

In the collecting duct, water movement is controlled by antidiuretic hormone, which opens the water channels. Aldosterone has a different job: it drives sodium and potassium handling in the late distal tubule and collecting duct. Quick way to keep them apart: antidiuretic hormone is the water hormone, aldosterone is the sodium-for-potassium hormone.

cards.t: Loop diuretics: mechanism and drugs
q: how do loop diuretics work
which drugs are loop diuretics
why are loop diuretics so potent
cards.x:
Loop diuretics are the most potent diuretics. They block the sodium-potassium-2 chloride carrier on the inside surface of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This stretch takes back about 25 percent of the sodium. The carrier normally pulls in sodium, potassium and two chlorides together. When it is blocked, they stay in the tube and leave in the urine, and water goes with them. That gives the biggest rise in urine flow of any class, up to 4 liters a day.

There are four: furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide (Bumex), torsemide (Demadex) and ethacrynic acid (Edecrin). Ethacrynic acid is the one that doesn't follow the "-ide" naming pattern. Loops also waste calcium and magnesium. Normally potassium leaking back into the tube keeps it positively charged, and that charge drives magnesium and calcium back into the blood. Blocking the carrier disrupts this, which is why loops waste both.

cards.t: Uses of loop diuretics and why they still work in poor kidney function
q: when are loop diuretics used
why do loop diuretics work when kidney function is low
how are loop diuretics used for hypercalcemia
cards.x:
Loops are used mainly when a lot of salt and water has to come off. The listed uses are:
- pulmonary edema (they lower pressure in the lungs)
- nephrotic syndrome (protein loss means the plasma cannot hold its fluid)
- cirrhosis of the liver (for ascites)
- heart failure, renal failure or insufficiency, and hypertension

They can also be added alongside saline in hypercalcemia, because they increase calcium excretion. Saline hydration is the main treatment.

One feature sets them apart: they stay effective when the creatinine clearance is below 30 milliliters per minute. A patient making urine does not necessarily have kidneys that are working well, but the loops can still get that urine flowing. Thiazides, by contrast, mostly lose their effect at that point.

cards.t: Loop diuretics and low potassium, calcium and magnesium
q: why do loop diuretics cause hypokalemia
which electrolytes do loop diuretics lower
why is potassium important with diuretics
cards.x:
Loop diuretics lower potassium, calcium and magnesium because they increase the excretion of all three. Low potassium (hypokalemia) can cause weakness and cardiac arrhythmias, and low calcium and low magnesium (hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia) come along with it. Low sodium (hyponatremia) is also listed, with seizures as the concern.

Potassium is the one to respect, because potassium problems can kill a patient very easily. Diuretics don't all move it the same way: loops lower it, while some other diuretics raise it, so you have to know what each drug is doing to the patient's potassium.

cards.t: Other loop diuretic side effects and why they happen
q: why do loop diuretics cause high blood sugar
why do loop diuretics cause gout
what is contraction alkalosis
cards.x:
Beyond electrolytes, loops cause several metabolic problems, and each has a reason:
- Hyperglycemia (high blood sugar): low potassium impairs insulin release; the reflex release of catecholamines acts through alpha-2 receptors to cut insulin release and through beta-2 receptors to increase glycogen breakdown; and the tissues take up less glucose (insulin resistance).
- Gout (hyperuricemia): the proximal tubule reabsorbs more uric acid, less is secreted, and the shrunken plasma volume concentrates it.
- Contraction alkalosis (mild metabolic alkalosis): volume depletion raises bicarbonate reabsorption (a minor effect) and enhances hydrogen ion secretion (the major one).
- Mild hyperlipidemia: more sympathetic activity raises triglycerides.

The volume loss itself also switches on the renin-angiotensin system, aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone.

cards.t: Ototoxicity with loop diuretics and aminoglycosides
q: why do loop diuretics cause hearing problems
what happens when you give gentamicin with furosemide
cards.x:
Ototoxicity means damage to the hearing system. Loop diuretics such as furosemide can damage the cochlea, the hearing organ of the inner ear. This is a listed adverse effect. It is classically described as hair-cell damage, though the effect is often reversible. In practice it is seen mainly with rapid high-dose intravenous use, kidney failure and aminoglycoside use.

That last one is a drug interaction. Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin can damage hearing themselves, and a loop diuretic potentiates that ototoxicity, so the combination is risky. A patient on a loop diuretic should report any hearing problems.

cards.t: Loop diuretic drug interactions
q: what drugs interact with loop diuretics
why do nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs weaken loop diuretics
why is a loop diuretic dangerous with digoxin
cards.x:
Five interactions are worth knowing for loop diuretics:
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs blunt the salt-loss and blood pressure response. Loops stimulate prostaglandin E2 (part of their vasodilating action), and these drugs block prostaglandins.
- Aminoglycosides: ototoxicity is potentiated.
- Warfarin: the two compete for plasma protein binding.
- Lithium: lithium clearance falls and its toxicity rises.
- Digitalis drugs such as digoxin: the low potassium and low magnesium that loops cause bring on arrhythmias.

The last one is why a heart failure patient on a loop diuretic and digoxin needs the potassium watched.

cards.t: Ethacrynic acid and the loop diuretic boxed warning
q: what is different about ethacrynic acid
do loop diuretics have a boxed warning
which loop diuretic can be used in a sulfonamide allergy
cards.x:
Furosemide, bumetanide and ethacrynic acid carry a US Food and Drug Administration boxed warning. These are potent diuretics which, in excessive amounts, can lead to a profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion.

Ethacrynic acid is the odd one out in other ways too. Its name doesn't follow the "-ide" pattern of the other loops. It is the loop diuretic that does not contain a sulfonamide group, which matters in a sulfonamide-allergic patient. And it is the loop most associated with ototoxicity (damage to hearing).

cards.t: When to be careful with loop diuretics (contraindications)
k: who should not take loop diuretics
q: what are the contraindications of loop diuretics
when should loop diuretics be avoided
what should be checked before giving a loop diuretic
cards.x:
Apart from anuria (no urine output) and known allergy to the drug, there is no separate contraindication list for loop diuretics. So their adverse effects are the working guide. The situations to avoid or monitor are:
- volume depletion (they already remove salt and water)
- gout (they raise uric acid)
- uncontrolled diabetes (they can raise blood sugar)
- low potassium in a patient taking a digitalis drug such as digoxin, because the low potassium and low magnesium bring on arrhythmias

Poor kidney function does not make them useless: loops still work when the creatinine clearance is below 30 milliliters per minute.

cards.t: Thiazide diuretics: mechanism and drugs
q: how do thiazide diuretics work
which drugs are thiazides
where do thiazides act in the nephron
cards.x:
Thiazides block the sodium-chloride transporter on the inside surface of the distal convoluted tubule. Blocking it gives a moderate diuresis, because this stretch of tubule handles only about 5 percent of the sodium. Thiazides inhibit up to 5 percent of the filtered sodium and chloride. They raise urine output by 1 to 2 liters a day, compared with up to 4 liters for a loop. They also increase potassium and magnesium excretion.

The group, which includes thiazide-like drugs, is chlorothiazide (Diuril), hydrochlorothiazide (Aquazide), chlorthalidone (Hygroton), metolazone (Mykrox) and indapamide (Lozol). Thiazides also have minor side actions on carbonic anhydrase and, at high dose, on phosphodiesterase, but those are not the ones to learn.

cards.t: Thiazides for high blood pressure
q: why are thiazides used for hypertension
who responds best to thiazide diuretics
are thiazides first line for high blood pressure
cards.x:
Thiazides are the diuretics used for long-term (chronic) high blood pressure. They suit elderly patients, African American patients and sodium-retentive states, because getting rid of that extra sodium reduces the "waterlogging" of the body. Low doses are preferred because they cause few adverse effects, and they are well tolerated and cheap. Their effect lasts longer than a loop's, which is why thiazides, not loops, are used for chronic hypertension.

Their mechanism changes over time. In the short term they decrease blood volume and cardiac output. Chronically they relax the vessels directly, so total peripheral resistance falls: there is less sodium in the arteriolar walls, so the wall is thinner and the diameter larger, and the vessel responds less to norepinephrine. Current US hypertension guidelines still list thiazide-type diuretics among the first-line drug classes, alongside angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and calcium channel blockers.

cards.t: Thiazides, calcium and kidney stones
q: why do thiazides raise calcium but prevent kidney stones
do thiazides treat hypercalcemia
how do thiazides differ from loops in calcium handling
cards.x:
Thiazides do the opposite of loops with calcium: they decrease calcium excretion in the urine, because calcium reabsorption rises in both the proximal tubule and the distal tubule. Two things follow. Serum calcium creeps up a little (hypercalcemia is a listed adverse effect, though a minor bump), and there is less calcium left in the urine to crystallize.

That resolves the apparent paradox: a drug that raises blood calcium is used to prevent calcium oxalate kidney stones, in patients who lose too much calcium in the urine. Thiazides are not a treatment for hypercalcemia. Loops with saline are, because loops waste calcium.

cards.t: Thiazide diuretic adverse effects
q: what are the side effects of thiazide diuretics
why do thiazides cause gout
why do thiazides cause hypokalemia
cards.x:
Thiazides cause many of the same problems as loops, usually less intensely (calcium is the exception: thiazides raise it a little, while loops lower it):
- Volume depletion, with reflex responses and orthostatic symptoms such as dizziness on standing, falling blood pressure and dry mouth. The reflexes include more sympathetic activity and more renin-angiotensin, aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone activity.
- Hypokalemia (they increase potassium excretion), which predisposes to cardiac arrhythmias.
- Metabolic alkalosis, from the contracted extracellular fluid.
- Hyperuricemia and gout, because of volume contraction and less uric acid excretion.
- Hyperglycemia (decreased glucose tolerance and insulin secretion) and hypercalcemia.
- Hyperlipidemia, a 5 to 15 percent rise in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
- Allergic skin rashes, photosensitivity, dizziness, headache, weakness, restlessness, sexual dysfunction and constipation.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs also weaken them, because prostaglandins aid natriuresis (salt loss). And thiazides increase digitalis toxicity, so potassium should be kept above 4.0 milliequivalents per liter.

cards.t: Thiazides at low creatinine clearance (metolazone)
q: do thiazides work in kidney failure
why is metolazone different from other thiazides
which diuretic works at low creatinine clearance
cards.x:
Thiazides become ineffective when the creatinine clearance drops too low, below about 30 to 40 milliliters per minute. The exception is metolazone, which still works at very low clearances. One way to remember it: metolazone could make a rock pee. One example of use: a volume-overloaded heart failure patient is already on a furosemide drip, and metolazone is added.

Hold this loosely rather than as an absolute. Newer trial data show that chlorthalidone also works in advanced kidney disease, so don't memorize "thiazides never work in kidney disease." Loops, in contrast, keep working below a creatinine clearance of 30.

cards.t: Loop versus thiazide diuretics (comparison)
k: difference between loop and thiazide diuretics
q: what is the difference between loop and thiazide diuretics
which diuretic wastes calcium and which keeps it
cards.x:
Both lower potassium and magnesium and both raise uric acid and blood sugar. The differences:
- Calcium: the loop wastes calcium (and treats hypercalcemia); the thiazide keeps calcium (and treats calcium stones).
- Kidney function: the loop works at a very low clearance; the thiazide mostly does not, except metolazone (newer data show chlorthalidone also works).
- Main job: the thiazide is the chronic hypertension drug; the loop is the volume-removal drug.
- Site and strength: loops act in the thick ascending limb and are the most potent; thiazides act in the distal tubule and give a moderate flow.

cards.t: Uses of thiazide diuretics (and what they are not for)
q: what are thiazides used for
do thiazides treat hypercalcemia
why are thiazides not used much in heart failure
cards.x:
Thiazides are used for hypertension, cirrhosis of the liver, heart failure and renal calcium stones (calcium oxalate). Hypertension is the main long-term use, with low doses preferred because they cause few adverse effects.

Three limits are worth knowing. Thiazides do not treat hypercalcemia: they raise serum calcium a little, and loops with saline are the ones used for that. They are not potent enough for most heart failure patients, which is why loops are the mainstay there. And they mostly lose their effect when kidney function is very low (creatinine clearance below about 30 to 40 milliliters per minute), with metolazone the exception; newer data show chlorthalidone also works in advanced kidney disease.

cards.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene)
q: how do potassium-sparing diuretics work
which drugs are potassium-sparing diuretics
why are potassium-sparing diuretics combined with other diuretics
cards.x:
Potassium-sparing diuretics are modest diuretics that block sodium channels in the collecting duct and so hold on to potassium. The drugs are amiloride (Midamor; the combination is Moduretic) and triamterene (Dyrenium; the combinations are Dyazide and Maxzide). The combinations are with hydrochlorothiazide. Sodium normally enters the collecting duct cells through these channels while potassium leaves. Blocking them inhibits 2 to 3 percent of sodium chloride reabsorption and decreases the gradient for potassium secretion. Potassium is held on to, which is the "sparing".

Because the diuretic effect is modest, they are used for the same conditions as other diuretics. Most often they are used in combination with other diuretics or antihypertensive drugs. A loop plus a potassium-sparing diuretic is a deliberate pairing: it offsets the potassium a loop wastes.

cards.t: Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics
q: what is the main side effect of potassium-sparing diuretics
why avoid potassium supplements with triamterene
which drugs add to hyperkalemia with amiloride
cards.x:
High serum potassium (hyperkalemia) is the main adverse effect of potassium-sparing diuretics. They hold on to potassium by design, so anything else that raises potassium stacks on top: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and potassium supplements. A potassium supplement should be avoided unless the prescriber says otherwise, because the combination can push potassium dangerously high. Amiloride and triamterene carry a US Food and Drug Administration boxed warning for hyperkalemia.

Other listed adverse effects: glucose intolerance in diabetes, megaloblastic anemia with triamterene and azotemia (raised blood urea nitrogen) with amiloride.

cards.t: Salt substitutes and potassium
q: why are salt substitutes a problem with potassium-sparing diuretics
what is in a salt substitute
cards.x:
Salt substitutes are usually potassium chloride. Potassium chloride tastes salty enough (with a slightly bitter edge) to stand in for salt. So a salt substitute cuts the sodium a patient eats, which is why someone on a low-sodium diet may be given one. The catch is that it adds potassium.

So a patient on a potassium-sparing diuretic, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker has to be cautious. Each of these already pushes potassium up, and a salt substitute adds to the hyperkalemia risk. This is a point of patient education for those drugs.

cards.t: What aldosterone does in the kidney
q: what does aldosterone do
why does excess aldosterone cause hypokalemia
how does aldosterone work in the collecting duct
cards.x:
Aldosterone is the major mineralocorticoid ("mineral" means salt). It is made by the adrenal cortex. The kidney's renin starts the chain that releases it. In a collecting-duct cell, aldosterone binds its receptor, which moves into the nucleus and switches on protein synthesis. That raises the number of sodium channels in the membrane and the activity of the sodium-potassium pump. It also stimulates energy production in the distal convoluted tubule.

More sodium channels means sodium and water are reabsorbed while potassium is lost, which is why chronic excess aldosterone (hyperaldosteronism) produces hypokalemia. There are two ways to interrupt this chain: block the sodium channels (amiloride and triamterene) or block aldosterone itself (aldosterone antagonists).

cards.t: Aldosterone antagonists: spironolactone and eplerenone
q: how do aldosterone antagonists work
what are spironolactone and eplerenone used for
why do aldosterone antagonists cause hyperkalemia
cards.x:
Aldosterone antagonists, spironolactone (Aldactone) and eplerenone (Inspra), are drugs that block aldosterone's receptor. They bind the steroid receptor that aldosterone uses but don't move on to the nucleus. Picture aldosterone as a message and the receptor as a mailbox: the drug jams the mailbox, so the message to build more sodium channels never arrives. They block 2 to 3 percent of sodium chloride reabsorption, so the flow is modest, but the sodium-for-potassium swap stops and potassium is spared. They work best when aldosterone is high.

Uses: primary aldosteronism, hypertension, heart failure, edematous conditions, nephrotic syndrome, and cirrhosis, which causes secondary hyperaldosteronism. The danger is hyperkalemia (with mild acidosis). With an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor such as lisinopril, both drugs raise potassium, so the risk is high and potassium must be monitored.

cards.t: Spironolactone's breast and menstrual side effects (switch to eplerenone)
q: why does spironolactone cause gynecomastia
when should you switch from spironolactone to eplerenone
is spironolactone an androgen blocker
cards.x:
Spironolactone is an androgen receptor antagonist: it blocks the receptor for male hormones, and it also modestly lowers androgen production, so it lowers androgen action in everyone. That explains its side effects: gynecomastia (breast enlargement) in men and menstrual irregularity in women.

The same antiandrogen action is why it is used to treat hirsutism (excess hair) and acne. Hirsutism is a use, not a side effect, and masculinizing effects are not expected from it.

Eplerenone binds the androgen receptor much less, so if a patient has breast enlargement or menstrual problems on spironolactone, the answer is to switch to eplerenone. Spironolactone is older and cheaper, so it is tried first.

cards.t: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: mechanism and drugs
q: how do carbonic anhydrase inhibitors work
why are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors weak diuretics
which drugs are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
cards.x:
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are weak diuretics that block an enzyme in the proximal tubule that runs the recycling of bicarbonate. The drugs are acetazolamide (Diamox), dichlorphenamide (Daramide) and methazolamide (Glauctabs). Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate absorption in the proximal tubule fall by 80 to 90 percent, hydrogen ion production fall and the sodium-hydrogen exchange fall. The bicarbonate is stranded in the tube and passed in the urine, which makes the urine alkaline.

The short-term effect is to increase sodium and potassium excretion by about 5 percent. After 3 to 5 days it fades to 1 to 3 percent, because the rest of the nephron makes up for it. That is why they are the weakest diuretics.

cards.t: Metabolic acidosis from carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and their other uses
q: why do carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause metabolic acidosis
what is acetazolamide used for
why does acetazolamide help altitude sickness
cards.x:
Because bicarbonate is lost in the urine, the blood turns slightly acidic and the urine alkaline. That is a metabolic acidosis, unlike loops and thiazides, which cause a contraction alkalosis. The listed adverse effects are metabolic acidosis, potassium depletion and drowsiness (neurons fire less readily). Monitoring follows: watch for low bicarbonate and low potassium.

They have other uses too, two of which lean on the acidosis:
- Mountain (altitude) sickness: acidic blood makes the patient breathe faster, until the body adapts.
- Epilepsy: acidifying the blood hyperpolarizes neurons, making it harder for them to fire and cause a seizure.
- Glaucoma: bicarbonate in the ciliary body falls, so less aqueous humor forms. The topical forms are dorzolamide (Trusopt) and brinzolamide (Azopt).

cards.t: Causes of heart failure
q: what are the causes of heart failure
what is the most common cause of heart failure
cards.x:
Heart failure means the heart can't pump enough blood for the body's needs. Ischemic heart disease, including myocardial infarction (heart attack), accounts for 50 to 60 percent of cases.

The others are hypertension (chronic high blood pressure) and drug-induced heart failure. Two more are idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (a dilated heart muscle disease with no known cause) and other cardiomyopathies (alcoholic, viral and hypertrophic). Alcohol and heavy metals such as cobalt can also cause it.

cards.t: Systolic versus diastolic heart failure
q: what is the difference between systolic and diastolic heart failure
can ejection fraction be normal in heart failure
what causes diastolic dysfunction
cards.x:
Heart failure comes in two types, depending on which half of the heartbeat is failing. (Ejection fraction is the share of its blood the ventricle pushes out with each beat.)
- Systolic dysfunction is a problem of contraction: decreased contractility from loss of heart muscle, left ventricular hypertrophy (thickening) or dilated cardiomyopathies. It is assessed as reduced ejection fraction.
- Diastolic dysfunction is a problem of relaxation: the ventricle fills less, so cardiac output falls. Causes are left ventricular hypertrophy, because thicker, stiffer ventricles relax less efficiently, and ischemia, which impairs removal of calcium from the cytosol back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

The way to hold the difference: in diastolic failure the ejection fraction percentage may look fine, but the ventricle filled with less blood, so the total blood pumped (the cardiac output) is still down. Learn "reduced ejection fraction" rather than a cutoff number.

cards.t: Compensation in heart failure (the vicious circle)
q: how does the body compensate for heart failure
why do the compensations make heart failure worse
why does vasoconstriction increase afterload
cards.x:
When the heart fails, cardiac output (the amount of blood the heart pumps) falls and the body tries to make up for it. It increases preload (by retaining sodium and water), constricts vessels, speeds the heart rate and increases contractility (through sympathetic activation), and the left ventricle thickens (hypertrophy).

The trouble is that each response worsens the failure, so it becomes a vicious circle. Congestion and edema build up, causing shortness of breath, including when lying flat (orthopnea). Tissue perfusion falls, causing weakness and fatigue. Sympathetic and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation speed the heart further and constrict vessels, raising afterload (the resistance the ventricle pumps against), and more sodium and water are held. The drugs in this area each break the circle at a different point.

cards.t: What tips heart failure into decompensation, and nondrug therapy
q: what causes heart failure to get worse
what lifestyle measures help heart failure
how is heart failure treatment judged
cards.x:
Common precipitants of decompensation (a sudden worsening) are lack of compliance with treatment, uncontrolled hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, inadequate therapy, and inappropriate medications or fluid overload. Other causes are acute anginal chest pain, pulmonary infection and emotional stress. A typical example is the holiday season, when people travel, forget their medications and eat sodium-heavy food.

Nondrug therapy is to restrict dietary sodium and fluid. The exact figures vary between guidelines, but the point is to restrict both. Physical activity may improve functional status. Exercise capacity, meaning how much work the patient can do before getting winded, is also how efficacy is judged.

cards.t: Diuretics in heart failure (symptom relief only)
q: why are loop diuretics the mainstay of heart failure treatment
do diuretics improve survival in heart failure
why do heart failure patients weigh themselves daily
cards.x:
Loop diuretics are the mainstay of heart failure therapy. They decrease sodium and water retention, which decreases preload (the volume the heart has to pump), so the patient feels better. Thiazides are not potent enough for most heart failure patients.

But diuretics are for symptom relief only. There is no evidence that they slow progression or lower mortality, and they are not mandatory therapy. That is why some patients take them as needed: they weigh themselves daily, and a gain of more than a pound a day over several days is fluid, not tissue, which is the cue to take the loop. Weight gain over several days is how worsening fluid overload shows up.

cards.t: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors in heart failure
q: why are ACE inhibitors mandatory in heart failure
what are the problems with ACE inhibitors
what do you do if an ACE inhibitor causes cough
cards.x:
An angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker is mandatory in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (a weak pumping heart), because it prolongs survival. It works on every part of the problem. It decreases preload, afterload and sympathetic activation. It also decreases left ventricular hypertrophy, dilation and remodeling. The benefits are hemodynamic improvement, better exercise tolerance, fewer symptoms, fewer hospital admissions, slower progression and longer survival.

The problems to watch for are impaired kidney function, hypotension, a rise in serum potassium, cough and angioedema. So kidney function and potassium are monitored. If cough or angioedema is the problem, switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker. Both drug groups also carry a boxed warning for fetal toxicity.

cards.t: The three beta blockers that help in heart failure
q: which beta blockers are used in heart failure
why were beta blockers once contraindicated in heart failure
do all beta blockers reduce mortality in heart failure
cards.x:
Beta blockers were classically considered contraindicated in heart failure. They lower heart rate and contractility, and a failing heart can decompensate. Yet three of them have a mortality benefit: carvedilol (Coreg), metoprolol succinate (the extended-release form) and bisoprolol (Zebeta). Carvedilol is a third-generation beta blocker. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction these three are mandatory because they prolong survival. The other beta blockers have not been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure.

The benefits are better exercise tolerance, hemodynamic improvement (a higher ejection fraction), slower progression, fewer hospitalizations, less need for transplant and lower mortality. They are first-line therapy for patients with class II to IV heart failure. Patients should be on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker irrespective of symptoms. Metoprolol also carries a boxed warning against abrupt cessation.

cards.t: Starting beta blockers in heart failure (low and slow)
k: start low go slow beta blocker
q: how are beta blockers started in heart failure
why start beta blockers at a low dose in heart failure
how long does beta blocker titration take
cards.x:
Beta blockers are started low and increased slowly. The patient should be stable before starting. The starting dose is very low, and it is titrated up gradually, over a total of about 6 to 8 weeks, while watching for signs and symptoms of worsening heart failure. Starting in hospital is often preferred, but beta blockers can also be started in the outpatient clinic. The lesson is a very low dose in a stable patient, increased slowly.

The reason is that beta blockers lower heart rate and contractility, and a decompensating patient can die from an abrupt fall in both. It is a marathon, not a sprint. Patients should report worsening heart failure symptoms.

cards.t: How digoxin works
q: what is the mechanism of digoxin
how does digoxin increase the force of contraction
what are the neurohormonal effects of digoxin
cards.x:
Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside. Digoxin and digitalis-type compounds come from plants such as foxglove, lily of the valley and oleander. A lactone ring and a steroid nucleus are essential for activity. The attached sugar molecules influence absorption, half-life and metabolism.

It has two described actions. The older one is inotropic (stronger contraction). Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium pump of the heart muscle cell, so intracellular sodium rises. That weakens the sodium-calcium exchanger's normal removal of calcium from the cell. So calcium builds up and more is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the contraction is stronger.

The newer one is neurohormonal, working through nerves and hormones. Its effects are:
- less sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and more parasympathetic (slow-down) activity
- a resensitized baroreflex (the reflex that adjusts heart rate to blood pressure, so the rate falls)
- more parasympathetic activity in the atrioventricular node
- lower blood pressure, and less renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity with less remodeling
- better tissue perfusion and higher cardiac output

cards.t: Digoxin's place in heart failure treatment and its narrow window
q: does digoxin improve survival in heart failure
when is digoxin used
why is digoxin dangerous
what is the digoxin target level
cards.x:
Digoxin helps heart failure patients feel better but not live longer. The clinical benefits are better symptoms, exercise tolerance and quality of life and fewer hospitalizations; there is no survival benefit and no evidence it slows progression. So it isn't mandatory like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and beta blockers. It is an add-on for symptomatic patients who are already on optimal doses of an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, a beta blocker and a diuretic. It can also be used for rate control in atrial fibrillation with heart failure, though beta blockers are the usual first choice.

It has a very narrow therapeutic index: you don't need much to get drastic effects, and it is easy to get too much. A blood level is checked (target 0.5 to 1 nanogram per milliliter; higher levels may be linked to worse outcomes). What matters more than the exact number is that a level is monitored. It is cleared by the kidneys, so it accumulates in kidney problems.

cards.t: Signs of digoxin toxicity
q: what are the signs of digoxin toxicity
what does xanthopsia mean
what do you do when you suspect digoxin toxicity
cards.x:
Digoxin toxicity shows up in four places:
- Gut: anorexia and nausea.
- Vision: blurred vision, photophobia, xanthopsia (seeing yellow), shining lights around objects and yellow-green halos.
- Brain: delirium, fatigue, confusion, dizziness and abnormal dreams.
- Heart: nodal slowing with a longer PR interval (slower conduction from the atria to the ventricles), a shorter QT interval and a depressed ST segment. Bradycardia is classically listed as the most common, and premature ventricular beats are also very common, but just about any arrhythmia can occur; the ventricles become more sensitive, which is why premature ventricular beats are a clue.

Yellow-green halos with xanthopsia are a strong clue for digoxin, and the next step is to check a digoxin level right away. Treat it as a strong clue, not an absolute, because ivabradine can also cause halos.

cards.t: Digoxin halos versus ivabradine halos
q: how do you tell digoxin halos from ivabradine halos
what causes halos around lights in heart failure drugs
cards.x:
Halos around lights can come from digoxin or from ivabradine, so look at the rest of the picture.
- Digoxin gives a yellow-green tint to vision (xanthopsia) with halos. Other signs are blurred vision, nausea, confusion and a slow or irregular pulse, in a patient with a high digoxin level. The next step is a digoxin level.
- Ivabradine gives transient brightness in a limited part of the visual field (phosphenes), halos and multiple images, in a patient taking ivabradine. It can resolve on its own.

Halos around lights also occur in eye disease such as glaucoma and cataract. So yellow-green halos are a strong clue for digoxin but not an absolute one.

cards.t: Why low potassium makes digoxin more toxic
q: what electrolyte problems increase digoxin toxicity
why does low potassium increase digoxin toxicity
why do loop diuretics raise the risk of digoxin toxicity
cards.x:
Low potassium (hypokalemia), low magnesium (hypomagnesemia) and high calcium (hypercalcemia) all make digoxin toxicity more likely. Potassium is the clearest case: it competes with digoxin at the sodium-potassium pump, so when potassium is low, more digoxin binds.

This is why a heart failure patient on a loop diuretic needs the potassium watched: loops and thiazides waste potassium and magnesium, which increases digitalis toxicity, and potassium should be kept above 4.0 milliequivalents per liter. Add an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a potassium supplement and it gets complicated, because those push potassium the other way. High potassium is not a risk factor for digoxin toxicity; a very high potassium in acute overdose marks severe poisoning, which is a different point.

cards.t: Contraindications to digoxin
q: when should digoxin not be used
why is digoxin contraindicated in heart block
why is digoxin dangerous with ventricular tachycardia
cards.x:
The contraindications fall into two groups.
- Conduction and rate: advanced atrioventricular block, severe bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Digoxin increases parasympathetic activity at the atrioventricular node and slows the heart. So it adds to the slowing already present in advanced block, severe bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is also a listed contraindication.
- Ventricular rhythm: premature ventricular beats and ventricular tachycardia, because digoxin makes the ventricles more irritable.

Electrolyte disturbances also make toxicity more likely, so low magnesium, high calcium and low potassium are listed as risk factors.

cards.t: Digoxin immune Fab (the antidote)
q: what is the antidote for digoxin toxicity
how does digoxin immune Fab work
what is a risk of reversing digoxin
cards.x:
Digoxin immune Fab is the antidote for digoxin toxicity. Fab stands for fragment antigen-binding, the part of an antibody that grips its target. It is an antibody fragment made by immunizing healthy sheep with digoxin coupled to human serum albumin. The current brand is DigiFab.

Its affinity for digoxin is higher than the affinity of digoxin for the sodium-potassium pump. So it pulls the drug off the pump and rapidly reverses the toxicity. One caution: it can unmask whatever the digoxin was treating. The patient may go back into atrial fibrillation or have a heart failure decompensation, though that is better than the alternative.

cards.t: Spironolactone and eplerenone in heart failure
q: do spironolactone and eplerenone help in heart failure
who is not eligible for spironolactone in heart failure
what should you monitor with an aldosterone antagonist
cards.x:
Spironolactone and eplerenone reduce mortality in advanced heart failure, class III or IV. The mechanism is neurohormonal inhibition: blocking aldosterone slows remodeling of the left ventricle and so slows progression of heart failure.

The danger is hyperkalemia, so serum potassium is the value to follow. They are avoided with a high potassium or a high serum creatinine, because with kidney dysfunction hyperkalemia and arrhythmias are more likely. For spironolactone the cutoffs are a potassium above 5 milliequivalents per liter or a serum creatinine above 2.5. Spironolactone causes gynecomastia (breast enlargement) in about 10 percent of men. Eplerenone rarely does, so breast effects are the reason to switch to eplerenone.

cards.t: Milrinone and inamrinone (phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitors)
q: how does milrinone work
what is milrinone used for
why is milrinone only used short term
cards.x:
Milrinone (Primacor) and inamrinone (Inocor, formerly amrinone) are inotropes: drugs that make the heart contract harder. They inhibit phosphodiesterase type 3, the enzyme that breaks down cyclic adenosine monophosphate. So cyclic adenosine monophosphate is not broken down, rises in the heart and stimulates contraction directly. They also dilate arteries and veins in a balanced way, which decreases afterload and increases cardiac output.

They are approved only for short-term intravenous use in acute decompensated heart failure. That is because long-term use is associated with higher mortality and morbidity than placebo. Adverse effects are thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count, less likely with milrinone than with inamrinone) and ventricular arrhythmias.

cards.t: Dobutamine and dopamine, and choosing a short-term inotrope
q: what are dobutamine and dopamine used for
how do you choose between milrinone and dobutamine
why is dopamine used for low blood pressure in heart failure
cards.x:
Dobutamine is a selective beta-1 agonist. Given as an intravenous infusion, it stimulates the force of contraction more than the rate, and it is used short term to stabilize patients. Dopamine is also an intravenous infusion and acts through dopamine and beta receptors. Low-dose dopamine has not been shown to protect the kidney. Dopamine carries a boxed warning about tissue injury if the infusion leaks out of the vein.

The main question for choosing is the patient's blood pressure. If it is high, milrinone works better, because its balanced vasodilation lowers pressure. If it is low, dobutamine or dopamine make more sense, because they raise the force of contraction with much less vasodilation than milrinone. All of these are short term and started in hospital, because the longer a patient stays on them the more the risk of arrhythmia climbs.

cards.t: Ivabradine
q: how does ivabradine work
who gets ivabradine in heart failure
what are the side effects of ivabradine
cards.x:
Ivabradine (Procoralan) slows the heart rate without weakening contraction, which is how it differs from a beta blocker. It blocks the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel. This channel carries the pacemaker current in the sinoatrial node (the heart's natural pacemaker). It is for heart failure patients on the maximally tolerated beta blocker dose, in normal sinus rhythm, with a heart rate above 70 beats per minute. It works only in sinus rhythm, which is why atrial fibrillation matters.

It decreases hospitalization for worsening heart failure. It has not been shown to lower overall mortality, so it doesn't belong with the mandatory survival drugs. Adverse effects:
- a higher risk of atrial fibrillation (new palpitations)
- symptomatic bradycardia
- visual phosphenes (transient brightness in part of the visual field, halos and multiple images). These can resolve on their own, so the patient is reassured and asked to report persistent symptoms.

Contraindications resemble beta blockers': hypotension, heart block, a pacemaker and so on.

cards.t: Sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto)
q: how does sacubitril-valsartan work
why can't you give sacubitril-valsartan with an ACE inhibitor
what are the side effects of sacubitril-valsartan
cards.x:
Sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto) combines a neprilysin inhibitor with valsartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker. Neprilysin normally breaks down vasoactive peptides such as natriuretic peptide and bradykinin. Inhibiting it causes vasodilation, natriuresis (salt loss) and diuresis, and it inhibits growth and fibrosis of heart tissue. It is used to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization in heart failure.

It must never be given with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor: allow a 36-hour washout. The main reason is angioedema, because both angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and neprilysin inhibition let bradykinin build up. So a history of angioedema is a contraindication. The most common adverse effects are hypotension, hyperkalemia, cough and renal insufficiency, so watch for low blood pressure and high potassium. It also carries a boxed warning for fetal toxicity (stop it when pregnancy is detected).

cards.t: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in heart failure
q: how do SGLT2 inhibitors help heart failure
what are the side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors
why do SGLT2 inhibitors cause yeast infections
cards.x:
Dapagliflozin (Farxiga) and empagliflozin (Jardiance) are sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. They were first made for diabetes: they block the sodium-glucose transporter in the proximal tubule, so the kidneys don't reabsorb glucose. In stable, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction they reduce mortality and hospitalizations, so they are a necessary add-on. They also help heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

The risks follow from how they work. Hypotension, because patients lose fluid. Fungal infections of the genitourinary tract (typically a genital yeast infection), because there is more sugar there. They also carry a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis that can occur with normal blood glucose. Patients are told to watch for dizziness from low blood pressure and for fungal infections.

cards.t: Heart failure drugs: symptom relief versus survival benefit
k: which heart failure drugs prolong life
q: which heart failure drugs improve survival
which heart failure drugs only treat symptoms
which heart failure drugs are mandatory
cards.x:
The rule: if a drug is good for mortality, you want the patient on it no matter what. If it is good only for symptoms, the patient may not need it all the time.
- Symptoms only: loop diuretics (and thiazides where strong enough) and digoxin.
- Survival benefit: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers; carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol; spironolactone and eplerenone in advanced failure; sacubitril-valsartan; and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors.
- On neither list: milrinone is short-term support for acute decompensation, and long-term use is associated with higher mortality. Ivabradine reduces hospitalization but has not been shown to lower overall mortality.

The survival evidence for these drugs comes from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

cards.t: Which drugs lower potassium and which raise it
q: which diuretics lower potassium
which heart failure drugs raise potassium
why is potassium so important with these drugs
cards.x:
Potassium problems can kill a patient, so each class needs to be filed as lowering or raising it.
- Lowers potassium: loop diuretics, thiazides and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, which increase potassium excretion or deplete it.
- Raises potassium: potassium-sparing diuretics, aldosterone antagonists, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and sacubitril-valsartan. Potassium supplements and salt substitutes (potassium chloride) add to it.

Some pairings are deliberate: a loop plus a potassium-sparing diuretic offsets the potassium a loop wastes. Others stack risk: a potassium-sparing diuretic or an aldosterone antagonist with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or a supplement. And low potassium raises digoxin toxicity, so you have to work out where the patient will end up.

cards.t: What to monitor with diuretics and heart failure drugs
q: what should be monitored with heart failure drugs
what labs are checked with diuretics and ACE inhibitors
what is monitored in a patient on digoxin
cards.x:
What gets watched depends on the drug:
- Daily weight: worsening fluid overload shows up as weight gain over several days, especially in heart failure patients on a loop diuretic.
- Potassium and kidney function: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors raise potassium and can impair kidney function; keep potassium above 4.0 milliequivalents per liter with a thiazide and digitalis; spironolactone is not for a potassium above 5 or a serum creatinine above 2.5.
- Beta blockers: start low in a stable patient, increase slowly and watch for worsening heart failure signs and symptoms.
- Digoxin level: checked, especially when toxicity is suspected.
- Milrinone, inamrinone, dobutamine and dopamine: started in hospital for acute decompensation and stopped as the patient stabilizes.
- Sacubitril-valsartan: a 36-hour washout after an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

cards.t: Drugs that change digoxin levels
q: what drugs interact with digoxin
what raises digoxin levels
does St. John's wort affect digoxin
cards.x:
Digoxin's blood level is shifted by several things. Amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine and macrolide antibiotics such as clarithromycin raise digoxin levels, and St. John's wort lowers them. Loop and thiazide diuretics matter too, but not by changing the level. They lower potassium and magnesium, and the hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia bring arrhythmias and increase digitalis toxicity. Digoxin is also cleared by the kidneys, so it builds up when kidney function is poor.

Because the therapeutic window is narrow, anything that raises the level or makes the heart more sensitive to it is a risk. That is why a level is checked when toxicity is suspected.

cards.t: Patient teaching for diuretics and heart failure drugs
k: what to tell patients on diuretics
q: what should patients know about diuretics
what should heart failure patients be told
what should patients on digoxin watch for
cards.x:
What patients are told, by drug:
- All heart failure patients: restrict sodium and fluid, weigh yourself every day, and report a gain over several days, which is fluid.
- Loop and thiazide diuretics: expect volume depletion and dizziness; photosensitivity and rash are possible; report hearing problems with a loop; gout and high blood sugar can occur; potassium and magnesium need monitoring.
- Potassium-sparing diuretics, aldosterone antagonists, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and sacubitril-valsartan: be cautious with potassium supplements and salt substitutes.
- Spironolactone: breast enlargement in men or menstrual irregularity in women is the reason to ask for eplerenone.
- Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: drowsiness.
- Digoxin: report nausea, loss of appetite, yellow-green halos or blurred vision, confusion and a slow pulse, which are signs of toxicity.
- Ivabradine: transient brightness, halos or multiple images can happen and may resolve on their own.
- Beta blockers in heart failure: started low, increased slowly; report worsening heart failure symptoms.
- Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors: dizziness from low blood pressure and fungal infections.
